header: ZU-MED-105 · Professional Practice I, 24 single-best-answer questions authored from mcq شامل.pdf pages 12-40, the third dispatch pass over this tier-2 bank (following pp1-cluster3's self-directed-learning pass over pages 2-11 and pp1-cluster4's first pass over the bioethics/consent/leadership/health-determinants sections). This pass picks up the ~60 items pp1-cluster4 triaged, keyed and explicitly deferred: law and culture definitions, the 'three main questions' and 'principles guide decision-making' all-of-the-above list items, a competent adult's right to decide about their own body, the equity-in-healthcare-principles all-of-the-above item, care for vulnerable populations, present-and-future-generations bioethics, stigmatization as a social concept, a UNESCO-style culture definition, performance indicators in education, the second leadership-skills list's all-of-the-above item, the performing stage of team dynamics, effective-team principles and challenges, the elements/stages-of-team-dynamics list, the importance of teamwork in healthcare, and the Health/Wellness/Spectrum-of-health trio on page 38. Keys recovered via the same yellow fill-rectangle highlight and ad hoc PyMuPDF detection method pp1-cluster3/4 validated for this source (page.get_drawings() non-white filled rectangles matched to the option-line bounding box the fill's vertical centre falls inside), spot-checked this pass against the same script's own page-2 validation run (4/4 marks matched exactly, 0 mismatches, confirming the script still functions correctly on this file). Two items are genuinely doubtful marks, both render-confirmed as printed and authored with the doubt recorded in field_notes.uncertainty rather than silently corrected or held, per this lane's standing rule: a page-15 item whose stem describes fair and equitable treatment of individuals within populations is marked 'Justice' rather than the more intuitive 'Equity' (its own page-22 internal-duplicate restates the same stem and the same mark); and a page-29 item whose stem is the standard 'affirmation and acceptance of diversity ... politics, science, medicine, religion' definition of pluralism (matching this same source's own page-28 pluralism item almost fact-for-fact) is instead marked 'Culture'. A third render-confirmed doubtful pair, the page-30 responsibility/accountability items that reverse the conventional self-initiated-vs-requested-by-another distinction relative to that same page's own conventional first item, is likewise authored with the doubt recorded rather than held, per this dispatch's explicit instruction. One item planned from the triage (page 19's 'Justice: fairness with respect to distribution of medical resources') turned out on search-before-mint to be a duplicate of lane 1's existing concept CON-POP-BED479E0FA27CA (justiceprinciple.fair-distribution-of-healthcare-resources, question pp1-zag24-q05) and is held rather than authored; see coverage/ZU-MED-105-LEDGER.md for this and every other held/deferred item this pass.

questions.title: Definition of law
questions.question: The system of rules which a particular country or community recognizes as regulating the actions of its members and which it may enforce by the imposition of penalties. Refer to

explanations.A: Correct. Law is defined here as the system of rules that a particular country or community recognizes as regulating the actions of its members, enforceable by the imposition of penalties. This enforceable, rule-based framing is what distinguishes law from culture, which this same source instead defines as the ways of life, arts, beliefs and institutions a population passes down across generations. Law and culture are introduced here as a paired distinction, since both can regulate behaviour but only law does so through recognised, penalty-backed rules.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Culture, tested separately in this source, is the ways of life, arts, beliefs and institutions passed down across generations, not the enforceable rule system this stem describes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Religion may inform a community's values, but it is not the enforceable system of rules with penalties that this stem specifically describes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Science is a method of inquiry, not a system of enforceable rules regulating a community's members.

questions.learning_objective: State that law is the system of rules a country or community recognizes as regulating its members' actions, enforceable by penalties.

questions.title: Definition of culture (ways of life)
questions.question: All the ways of life including arts, beliefs and institutions of a population that are passed down from generation to generation. Refer to

explanations.A: Incorrect. Law, tested separately in this source, is the enforceable system of rules a community recognizes, not the ways of life, arts, beliefs and institutions this stem describes.
explanations.B: Correct. Culture is defined here as all the ways of life, including arts, beliefs and institutions, of a population that are passed down from generation to generation. This is a broader, inherited-practice definition than law's enforceable rule-system, and it is the same basic sense of culture this module later builds on when it defines cultural diversity as more than one culture, race, language, tradition or religion coexisting in a society. Recognising culture as this inherited, multi-part bundle of practices is what this item specifically tests.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Religion is one component that can be passed down within a culture, but it alone does not capture the full arts-beliefs-institutions bundle this stem describes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Science is a method of inquiry, not the inherited ways of life, arts, beliefs and institutions this stem describes.

questions.learning_objective: State that culture is all the ways of life, including arts, beliefs and institutions, of a population passed down from generation to generation.

questions.title: The three main questions bioethics helps answer
questions.question: Bioethics helps us to answer three main questions include

options.A: What decisions are morally right or acceptable, alone.
options.B: How do we justify our decision in moral terms, alone.
options.C: The method or manner of our response when we act on our decision, alone.
options.D: What decisions are morally right or acceptable, how we justify our decision in moral terms, and the method or manner of our response when we act on our decision, together.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Identifying which decisions are morally right or acceptable is one of the three questions this source names, but alone it omits the other two this source groups together as the correct answer.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Justifying a decision in moral terms is one of the three questions this source names, but alone it omits the other two.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The method or manner of acting on a decision is one of the three questions this source names, but alone it omits the other two.
explanations.D: Correct. This source names three main questions bioethics helps answer together: which decisions are morally right or acceptable, how that decision is justified in moral terms, and the method or manner of the response when the decision is acted on. None of the three questions alone captures the complete three-part framework the source marks as correct. This all-of-the-above framing recurs throughout this source whenever it introduces a multi-part list rather than a single fact.

questions.learning_objective: State that bioethics helps answer three main questions together: which decisions are morally right or acceptable, how they are justified in moral terms, and the method of acting on them.

questions.title: Principles that guide medical decision making
questions.question: Some principles that guide medical decision making: include

options.A: Autonomy is not merely a right but also a responsibility, alone.
options.B: Most patients feel dependent on physicians, so respect for patients' autonomy by physicians is crucial, alone.
options.C: A health care provider is an expert in medicine, a patient is an expert in her/his preferences, beliefs and values, so patients have a right to refuse treatment but cannot claim all treatments, alone.
options.D: Autonomy is not merely a right but also a responsibility; most patients feel dependent on physicians so respect for their autonomy is crucial; and patients have a right to refuse treatment but cannot claim all treatments, together.

explanations.A: Incorrect. That autonomy is not merely a right but also a responsibility is one genuine principle this source lists, but alone it omits the other principles the source groups together as the correct answer.
explanations.B: Incorrect. That most patients feel dependent on physicians, making respect for their autonomy crucial, is one genuine principle this source lists, but alone it omits the others.
explanations.C: Incorrect. That patients have a right to refuse treatment but cannot claim all treatments is one genuine principle this source lists, but alone it omits the others.
explanations.D: Correct. This source lists three principles together as guiding medical decision making: autonomy is not merely a right but also a responsibility; most patients feel dependent on physicians, so physicians' respect for patient autonomy is crucial; and because a health care provider is an expert in medicine while a patient is the expert in their own preferences, beliefs and values, patients have a right to refuse treatment but cannot claim all treatments. None of the three principles alone captures the complete answer the source marks as correct. This complements this module's separate fact that, in medical decision making, the final word rests with the patient.

questions.learning_objective: State that principles guiding medical decision making include autonomy as both a right and a responsibility, the crucial role of respecting patient autonomy, and the patient's right to refuse but not to claim all treatments, together.

questions.title: A competent adult's right to decide about their own body
questions.question: A competent adult has the right to make decisions about what happens to his body. Refer to

explanations.A: Correct. This source keys a competent adult's right to make decisions about what happens to their own body to autonomy. This is a specific clinical application of autonomy, distinct from this module's separate, general definition of autonomy as the individual capacity for self-determination, independent decisions, actions and evaluations, applying that same capacity specifically to decisions about one's own body. Recognising bodily decision-making as an application of autonomy, not beneficence, non-maleficence or justice, is what this item tests.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Beneficence concerns a practitioner acting in a patient's best interest, not the patient's own right to decide about their body.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Non-maleficence concerns avoiding harm to a patient, not the patient's own right to decide about their body.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Justice concerns the fair distribution of resources, not an individual patient's right to decide about their own body.

questions.learning_objective: State that a competent adult's right to make decisions about what happens to their own body is an application of autonomy.

questions.title: Fair and equitable treatment of individuals within populations
questions.question: Is one of the basic principles of medical ethics. It is a concept intended to promote fair and equitable treatment of individuals within populations. Refer to

explanations.A: Incorrect. Autonomy concerns individual self-determination, not the population-level fair-treatment principle this stem describes.
explanations.B: Incorrect per this source's key, even though 'equity' is the more intuitive fit here: this module elsewhere defines equity specifically as identifying and giving people what they need, and 'fair and equitable treatment of individuals within populations' reads as a close paraphrase of that same idea. This source does not mark that option on this item, marking justice instead.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Equality, tested separately in this source, means giving everyone the same things regardless of need, a different framing from the fair-and-equitable-treatment-within-populations wording this stem uses.
explanations.D: Correct as keyed by this source, though it is a genuinely surprising mark: justice is presented here as the basic principle intended to promote fair and equitable treatment of individuals within populations, a description that reads more naturally as this module's own definition of equity (trying to identify and give people what they need). This exact stem and mark recur verbatim later in this same source (its own internal near-duplicate of the bioethics-principles block), so the mark is not a one-off slip. It is render-confirmed as genuinely printed rather than a detection artefact, so it stands per corpus policy on printed keys, flagged here for reviewer attention rather than silently corrected.

questions.learning_objective: State that this source marks 'fair and equitable treatment of individuals within populations' as a description of justice, though it reads as closer to this module's own definition of equity.

questions.title: Principles of equity in health care
questions.question: Principles of equity in health care. Refer to…….

options.A: Equity in health implies that ideally everyone should enjoy full health potential, and no one should be disadvantaged from this potential, alone.
options.B: Equal access and utilization of available care for equal need, alone.
options.C: Equal quality of care for everyone, alone.
options.D: Everyone enjoying full health potential without disadvantage, equal access and utilization of available care for equal need, and equal quality of care for everyone, together.

explanations.A: Incorrect. That everyone should ideally enjoy full health potential without disadvantage is one genuine principle this source lists, but alone it omits the other principles the source groups together as the correct answer.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Equal access and utilization of available care for equal need is one genuine principle this source lists, but alone it omits the others.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Equal quality of care for everyone is one genuine principle this source lists, but alone it omits the others.
explanations.D: Correct. This source lists three principles of equity in health care together: everyone should ideally enjoy full health potential without disadvantage, there should be equal access and utilization of available care for equal need, and there should be equal quality of care for everyone. None of the three principles alone captures the complete answer the source marks as correct. These principles apply this module's own definition of equity, identifying and giving people what they need, specifically to the health-care setting.

questions.learning_objective: State that principles of equity in health care include full health potential without disadvantage, equal access and utilization of care for equal need, and equal quality of care for everyone, together.

questions.title: Bioethical issues across present and future generations
questions.question: Bioethical issues should be considered

options.A: Not only for the present generation but also for future generations.

explanations.A: Correct. This source keys bioethical issues as needing consideration not only for the present generation but also for future generations. This forward-looking scope reflects that many bioethical questions, such as those concerning the environment, genetics or resource use, have consequences that extend well beyond the people currently alive. Limiting bioethical consideration to only the present or only the future would each miss half of the scope this source marks as correct.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Considering only the present generation omits the future-generations scope this source marks as necessary.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Considering only future generations omits the present-generation scope this source marks as necessary.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Only people living today" is a restatement of the present-generation-only option, which this source does not mark as sufficient on its own.

questions.learning_objective: State that bioethical issues should be considered not only for the present generation but also for future generations.

questions.title: Stigmatization as a social, not legal, concept
questions.question: The concept of "stigmatization" is…….

options.A: Social rather than a legal concept.
options.B: A social concept alone, with no further qualification.

explanations.A: Correct. This source keys stigmatization as a social rather than a legal concept. This complements this module's separate basic definition of stigmatization as a distinguishing mark or characteristic, adding that the mechanism by which such a mark leads to negative treatment operates through social processes and attitudes, not through formal legal categorisation. Distinguishing stigmatization's social nature from a legal one is what this item specifically tests, against the plainer restatement offered in option B.
explanations.B: Incorrect per this source's key: "a social concept" alone, without the explicit contrast to "legal", is not the option this source marks; the source specifically frames stigmatization against a legal concept, which is the comparison this item tests.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ethnicity is one basis on which stigmatization can occur, not a description of what kind of concept stigmatization itself is.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Religion is one basis on which stigmatization can occur, not a description of what kind of concept stigmatization itself is.

questions.learning_objective: State that the concept of stigmatization is a social rather than a legal concept.

questions.title: Culture: the set of spiritual, material, intellectual and emotional features of a society
questions.question: The set of distinctive spiritual, material, intellectual and emotional features of society or a social group and it encompasses, in addition to art and literature, lifestyles, ways of living together, value systems, traditions and beliefs.

options.B: Value of respect for cultural diversity

explanations.A: Correct. This source keys culture as the set of distinctive spiritual, material, intellectual and emotional features of a society or social group, encompassing art and literature, lifestyles, ways of living together, value systems, traditions and beliefs. This fuller, UNESCO-style definition complements this module's simpler, earlier definition of culture as the ways of life, arts, beliefs and institutions passed down across generations, spelling out in more detail what that inherited bundle of practices contains. Recognising this fuller enumeration as still describing culture, not one of the diversity-related terms tested alongside it, is what this item tests.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Value of respect for cultural diversity" names an attitude toward culture's existence, not the definition of culture itself that this stem describes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pluralism, tested separately in this source, is the affirmation and acceptance of diversity or the treatment of people as equal citizens, not this enumeration of a society's own spiritual, material, intellectual and emotional features.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Value-pluralism" is not the term this source keys to this enumeration of a society's own features.

questions.learning_objective: State that culture is the set of distinctive spiritual, material, intellectual and emotional features of a society, encompassing art, literature, lifestyles, value systems, traditions and beliefs.

explanations.C: Correct. Performing is the stage of team dynamics this source marks as the team focusing all its attention on achieving goals. This is the final, most resolved stage of the classic team-development sequence, following forming's ambiguity, storming's conflict, and norming's open communication and task-confronting. questions.title: Definition of health (WHO-style)
questions.question: It is a state of complete physical, mental, spiritual, and social well-being not merely the absence of disease or infirmity

explanations.A: Incorrect. Team dynamics, tested separately in this module, is the relationships and interactions between team members, unrelated to this definition of complete well-being.

explanations.C: Correct. Health is defined here, in the classic WHO-style formulation, as a state of complete physical, mental, spiritual and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. This positive, multi-dimensional definition is distinguished from wellness, which this same source instead defines as a healthy lifestyle with the ability and energy to do what one wants to do, and from spectrum of health, which frames health as a dynamic, continuously changing process rather than this fixed state. Health, wellness and spectrum of health are introduced together on this page as three related but distinct terms.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Wellness, tested separately in this source, describes a healthy lifestyle and the ability and energy to do what one wants, a related but distinct term from this complete-well-being definition of health itself.
